claims.text: Chemical complexity in Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni single crystals produces localized atomic-scale lattice distortions.
Localized lattice distortions generate heterogeneous barriers to dislocation slip.
These heterogeneous slip barriers predominantly govern the alloy's strength and deformation behavior.
The heterogeneous barriers increase the critical resolved shear stress required for dislocation motion relative to simpler alloys.
The proposed initial material is a well-annealed, macroscopically homogeneous Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni single crystal.
The Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy has inherent atomic-scale compositional fluctuations.
Thermal recovery is minimal near room temperature at moderate strain rates.
Under the stated conditions, dislocation motion is primarily controlled by local atomic distortions.
Chemically induced lattice distortions affect dislocation density and spatial distribution.
Chemically induced lattice distortions affect slip-band formation.
Chemical complexity causes atomic-size and elastic mismatch among constituent elements.
Atomic-size and elastic mismatch produce local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions act as irregularly spaced obstacles to dislocation motion.
The Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy will have a higher critical resolved shear stress than a simple FCC metal or simpler alloy tested under identical conditions.
The Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy will have greater strain-rate sensitivity than the simpler baseline.
Greater strain-rate sensitivity will be indicated by a higher activation energy obtained from thermal-activation fits.
TEM will reveal more heterogeneous dislocation structures in the multi-component alloy than in the simpler baseline.
TEM will reveal localized slip-band formation in the multi-component alloy.
The proposed mechanism should apply near room temperature and at moderate strain rates in compression-tested single crystals.
Using single crystals minimizes grain-boundary contributions to the measured deformation behavior.
